The early life history of Tridacna gigas is characterized by a brief embryonic period and rapid initial growth under the warm, stable conditions of tropical reef flats. Eggs are fertilized externally, and following a short period of development, the fertilised ovum transitions to a free-swimming veliger larva. In captive rearing studies conducted at a constant water temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], the age at birth, defined as the moment of hatching, occurs after only 0.83 days [ab = only 0.83 days]. This rapid hatching is followed by a lecithotrophic larval phase during which the larva relies entirely on residual yolk reserves. The time since birth at metamorphosis, marking the transition to a benthic juvenile, has been recorded as 7 days since birth  under these same thermal conditions at a temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C]. Immediately following settlement, the newly metamorphosed spat exhibit a growth rate at settlement of 0.033 centimeters per day , reflecting the swift onset of shell deposition at a temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C].

Juvenile growth in this species proceeds steadily during the first year post-settlement, with shell dimensions providing a clear record of ontogenetic development. Field surveys of wild populations inhabiting shallow lagoons at 30 °C [T = 30 °C] have documented that the shell length at 10 month reaches 2.6 centimeters , demonstrating a moderate juvenile growth phase. By 17 months, these same cohorts attain a shell length at 17 month of 8.3 centimeters , indicating an acceleration in growth rate as the juveniles transition to a more active filter-feeding lifestyle at a temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C]. This period of rapid expansion in shell dimensions is critical for outgrowing predation pressure from gastropods and fishes. The growth trajectory continues robustly into the sub-adult stage, with individuals reaching a shell length at 9 yr of 52 centimeters  when reared at 30 °C [T = 30 °C], a size that places them among the larger bivalves of the Indo-Pacific reef community.

Reproductive maturation in the giant clam is closely tied to the attainment of a minimum body size rather than strictly to age, a pattern common among slow-growing marine invertebrates. The onset of gametogenesis is triggered once an individual surpasses the shell length at puberty of 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters], after which gonadal tissue becomes macroscopically visible during histological examination. At this size, the clam begins allocating resources toward reproductive effort. Under optimal thermal conditions at 30 °C [T = 30 °C], the ultimate reproduction rate is realized through a high annual fecundity: gravid adults produce approximately 1,370,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,370,000 eggs per spawning event] and typically complete approximately 365 spawning events each year [F_R_i = approximately 365 spawning events each year], ensuring a massive output of gametes into the water column during synchronized mass-spawning events.

As the clam approaches its maximum size, the energetic demands of somatic growth diminish and resources are increasingly channeled into reproductive output. The ultimate shell height reaches 137 centimeters [Li = 137 centimeters], a dimension that makes Tridacna gigas the largest extant bivalve species. This immense final size is accompanied by a correspondingly large ultimate wet weight of 20,000 grams [Wwi = 20,000 grams], which includes the heavy calcified shell that can constitute over half of the total mass. At an intermediate benchmark, individuals measuring 115 centimeters in shell height possess a wet weight at 115 cm of 17,000 grams , indicating that much of the mass gain occurs in the final phases of growth as the shell thickens substantially. This formidable body size confers resistance to most predators, though large individuals may still fall prey to octopuses and certain triggerfish.

Longevity in this species is exceptional among tropical bivalves, with a lifespan that spans multiple decades. The maximum recorded longevity in wild populations maintained at 30 °C [T = 30 °C] is 100 years [am = 100 years], making the giant clam one of the longest-lived mollusks in coral reef ecosystems. Throughout this extended life, the clam must balance the high energetic costs of maintaining a massive body with the demands of annual spawning cycles. The initial investment in each new generation is remarkably small: the wet dry weight at birth of a newly hatched larva is only 0.000000523 grams [Wwb = 0.000000523 grams], derived from an egg with a diameter of approximately 100 micrometers. This minute starting mass, equivalent to the weight of a few algal cells, underscores the extraordinary magnitude of growth required to reach an adult mass nearly ten orders of magnitude greater, a feat made possible by decades of continuous filter-feeding and photosynthesis by symbiotic zooxanthellae.
